We present new observations of the nearby, gas-rich spiral galaxy UGC 8839, revealing a prominent, narrow hyper-stable disc (HSD) with a midplane H I column density of $\log(N_{\rm H\,I}) \approx 21.0$ cm$^{-2}$ and a vertical scale height of $h \approx 0.4$ kpc. This HSD extends from the galaxy's center outward to approximately 10 kpc, encompassing roughly 10% of the total H I mass. The structure is likely maintained by a combination of the galaxy's low central surface brightness and a low central stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma_{\star} \approx 20$ km s$^{-1}$), which together create a deep gravitational potential well. Theoretical models indicate that the HSD is sustained by a balance between the galaxy's gravitational pull and turbulent support, with a turbulent velocity of $v_t \approx 10$ km s$^{-1}$ and a Toomre $Q$ parameter near unity. The formation of the HSD may be driven by a lack of sufficient star formation to generate sufficient feedback to disrupt the disc, or it may result from feedback mechanisms that are insufficiently strong to prevent its maintenance. The presence of the HSD in UGC 8839 highlights the importance of studying such structures in nearby galaxies to better understand the processes governing gas accretion and

Paleo-detectors represent a proposed avenue for exploring dark matter (DM) interactions by analyzing the minute damage trails left in ancient geological formations. This study projects the capabilities of such devices by leveraging recent advancements in micro-tomography and atomic force microscopy. We anticipate that a 100-ton paleo-detector utilizing these technologies could probe spin-independent DM-nucleon cross-sections down to $10^{-50}$ cm$^2$ for dark matter masses exceeding 100 GeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these detectors could potentially surpass the sensitivities of next-generation direct detection experiments.

This study introduces a novel update mechanism for encrypted databases that leverages update-based differential privacy (DP) to conceal data modification patterns. In this framework, the DP parameters are defined such that a single database update must not significantly influence an adversary's ability to observe the overall update history. This approach is particularly advantageous compared to row-based DP, as it avoids the substantial privacy loss incurred by attackers inferring individual updates by comparing database snapshots before and after changes. The proposed solution ensures that any two possible data values within a specific update can differ only marginally in an attacker's view of the complete update log. We demonstrate the practicality of this method through a prototype implementation, showing that it remains feasible even when facing an omniscient adversary who has full knowledge of all updates except the specific one in question.

This paper introduces a novel method for determining feature importance within Random Forests by leveraging the Maximum Unsatisfiable Core (MUC) technique. Our approach involves retraining the original Random Forest with modified datasets where specific features are permuted or altered, subsequently utilizing MUC analysis of misclassified instances to assess feature significance. We conducted extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets to validate our method. Results indicate that our MUC-driven approach surpasses existing feature importance metrics, particularly excelling in scenarios where the Maximum Likelihood Classifier (MLC) is employed for decision-making. Furthermore, we propose an adversarial analysis framework based on our method to evaluate model robustness. Our findings demonstrate that this adversarial analysis effectively distinguishes between classifiers differing in robustness, such as the MLC versus the Softmax Maximum Likelihood Classifier (SMLC).

Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has become increasingly popular, yet it presents challenges regarding the loss of tactile feedback and a restricted field of view. To mitigate these issues, advanced visualization and image processing tools are essential. This study introduces a novel deep learning-based algorithm designed to segment surgical instruments in real time within laparoscopic video streams. The method employs a two-stage approach: first, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) extracts features from the raw endoscopic frames, and subsequently, a Random Forest classifier utilizes these features to isolate the instruments. The algorithm was evaluated on the Kvasir dataset, demonstrating a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 0.75 and a processing speed of 11.5 frames per second (FPS). These outcomes indicate that the proposed algorithm is well-suited for integration into surgical robotics systems to enhance the visualization of MIS procedures.

We introduce a novel, large-scale unsupervised person Re-Identification (ReID) method designed to generate discriminative ID-specific representations without relying on ID labels. Our approach utilizes contrastive learning to train a deep ID-specific encoder, initially processing unlabeled images through a pre-trained ID-agnostic encoder. To ensure effective ID separation, we employ a two-stage strategy: in the first stage, we cluster images into pseudo-labels using a k-means algorithm on ID-agnostic features, followed by supervised contrastive learning to optimize ID-agnostic features for better discrimination. In the second stage, we employ a contrastive learning framework that directly processes images to learn robust ID embeddings by pulling images of the same individual closer and pushing those of different individuals further apart. Extensive experiments conducted on two major ReID benchmarks demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art unsupervised approaches.

This paper introduces a novel measurement equation for threshold selection within Realized-GARCH models, utilizing a specific functional form for the realized conditional tail variance. By integrating these elements with conjugate priors, we derive the full posterior distribution and develop an efficient importance sampling scheme to approximate its moments. Empirical analysis confirms that the proposed Realized-GARCH framework, when equipped with this new realized threshold measurement equation, generates more accurate tail risk forecasts compared to both standard GARCH models and standard realized-GARCH models.

We introduce a Bayesian framework for determining the robust parameter estimates of pulsar timing residuals. This methodology treats systematic errors as nuisance parameters and employs a heavy-tailed probability distribution to model timing residuals. By utilizing robust posterior distributions, we derive reliable point estimates and their associated uncertainties. We compare these robust results with both standard robust estimators and conventional mean and covariance calculations. This analysis is conducted through Monte Carlo simulations, which demonstrate that the proposed robust estimators outperform traditional methods in scenarios involving outliers. Additionally, we apply this methodology to real data from the PSR 1855+09 pulsar to validate its practical utility.

We examine the correlation functions of pion currents composed of two quarks to analyze the behavior of pion constituents across varying temperatures and baryon chemical potentials. Our findings indicate that the pion's quark substructure remains largely intact up to $T_c$ in the vicinity of the crossover transition, even when the temperature is slightly above $T_c$. Furthermore, we observe a distinct enhancement in these correlations within the charm sector at temperatures exceeding $T_c$.

We conducted a comprehensive study of XX Cha's accretion variability by analyzing archival and new optical and near-infrared photometry, as well as new high-resolution spectroscopy. Our results reveal that XX Ac is a young star with a mass of approximately 0.8 solar masses, an age of roughly 10 million years, and a rotation period of 1.5 days. We detected a significant increase in accretion activity between May 2019 and May 2020, with the accretion rate rising by a factor of 100 from $1.1 \times 10^{-8}$ to $1.1 \times 10^{-6}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr. This dramatic change was accompanied by a 1.5 magnitude increase in the V-band and a 0.5 magnitude increase in the I-band, alongside a 100 K temperature rise in the accretion shock region. The analysis of our new and existing optical spectra indicates that the infall velocities of the accretion streams decreased from 300 km/s to 150 km/s during this event. The findings suggest that XX Cha's variability is driven by changes in the inner disk region, specifically a shift from a single high-velocity stream to a double stream configuration. This study investigates the redistribution of income to enhance individuals' opportunities, challenging the conventional view that such policies merely address existing income disparities. We introduce a novel framework for analyzing income redistribution by integrating the concept of opportunity inequality. Within this approach, we define an opportunity-based classification of income, where every earning is attributed to the opportunity bundle enabling its acquisition. We propose several criteria for optimal redistribution strategies, demonstrating that these methods apply broadly across various opportunity models and effectively encompass prior approaches utilizing individual-specific reference points. Additionally, we examine the implications of our model regarding progressive taxation and the allocation of government transfers.

We demonstrate that this object is isomorphic to the quantum $K$-theory, whereas for any finite group $W$, there exists an action of the group on the flag variety such that the ordinary $W$-theory of a flag variety is isomorphic to the representation ring of $W$. We introduce SHODAP, a novel framework designed to debug data issues within end-to-end machine learning pipelines. Recognizing that data quality problems are a primary driver of subpar model performance, existing methods have largely concentrated on diagnosing data flaws in isolation, overlooking their intricate interactions with the broader machine learning workflow. To address this gap, we propose a new definition of data importance grounded in Shapley value theory, specifically tailored for machine learning pipelines. This approach evaluates the significance of individual data points by quantifying their marginal contribution to the final model's output performance. We formalize these concepts and develop an efficient algorithm that approximates SHODAP scores with high precision, offering a practical alternative to the computationally prohibitive exact Shapley values. Empirical evaluations across three distinct datasets and various models demonstrate that SHODAP effectively identifies underlying data quality issues and the resulting model degradations. Furthermore, we validate our framework's utility in a real-world scenario using the Google News recommendation system, highlighting its practical application in production environments.

We present the initial findings from MAVERIC, a survey designed to identify radio sources in Galactic globular clusters (GCs). Utilizing the Arecibo Observatory, we conducted a deep survey of the core regions of 10 GCs, reaching a flux density limit of approximately 0.1 mJy. This dataset identifies 1,025 radio sources, with 1,015 being new discoveries. Our findings indicate that the cumulative number-flux density relation for these sources is consistent with that of the general stellar population in GCs, yet the sources are spatially segregated, clustering toward the central areas. Furthermore, the sources are divided into two distinct groups: a high-luminosity population ($S_{1.4\text{GHz}} > 10$ mJy) and a low-luminosity population ($S_{1.4\text{GHz}} < 10$ mJy). The high-luminosity group comprises 10 sources, 9 of which are associated with known millisecond pulsars (MSPs), while the remaining high-luminosity source is a radio-emitting white dwarf. Conversely, the low-luminosity group consists of 1,005 radio sources, 1,000 of which are newly identified. We argue that the high-luminosity sources represent the radio counterparts of X-ray binaries containing accreting neutron stars, whereas the low-luminosity sources

Graph learning has become increasingly vital, with numerous applications relying on graph neural networks (GNNs) to extract knowledge from graph structures. However, many real-world systems are inherently hypergraphs, where edges connect multiple nodes simultaneously. Conventional approaches typically flatten these hyperedges into pairwise connections, thereby discarding valuable higher-order structural information. Although some methods attempt to reconstruct hyperedges by leveraging edge features, they often yield poor results because the inherent pairwise relationships fail to capture the true complex interactions within a hyperedge. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for reconstructing hyperedges by explicitly modeling pairwise relationships that exist exclusively within each hyperedge. Our approach treats the formation of a hyperedge as a supervised learning task, where the goal is to predict membership of nodes based on their interactions. By introducing a new hypergraph convolutional network capable of capturing intricate pairwise dependencies, we enable the network to infer which nodes belong to the same hyperedge. Experiments across various real-world datasets demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces a directional emission metric based on differential entropy, designed to quantify the directional output of laser radiation. This metric is calculated using the far-field angular distribution of light emitted from a microcavity laser. The research examines how this differential entropy varies with the geometry of the mirror in a one-dimensional microcavity laser. The findings indicate that this metric serves as a practical tool for characterizing the directionality of light within such systems.

We examine the thermal atomic ensembles within the Dicke model, specifically analyzing the fluctuations of photon number in the thermally driven superradiant phase transition. Our findings indicate that photon number correlations are governed by the thermal state of the atoms, which, unlike a pure ground state, contains entanglement. Consequently, atomic-atom correlations in this thermal configuration generate non-classical photon statistics that deviate from those arising from pure quantum entanglement.

Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) focuses on learning multi-agent policies from fixed historical data. A prevalent challenge in offline MARL is that the generated actions within the dataset are often suboptimal, resulting in poor policy performance. This paper introduces a new offline MARL framework designed to enhance policy effectiveness by leveraging specific high-quality trajectories embedded in the dataset. We define a new metric, termed the "goodness" of a trajectory, to assess the proportion of steps within a trajectory that outperform the behavior policy. We demonstrate that the overall policy performance is bounded by this trajectory "goodness." Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm called T-Off-MADDPG, which operates offline and specifically targets the optimization of these high-quality trajectories. Extensive experiments confirm that T-Off-MADDPG significantly surpasses existing offline multi-agent methods.

We introduce a 2D/3D medical image registration framework designed to align kilovoltage (kV) images with treatment-planning computed tomography (CT) scans, thereby enhancing the geometric accuracy of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) treatments. To achieve this, we employed a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on a large dataset of 2D megavoltage (MV) images derived from 3D CT scans from the Medical Image Modeling Challenge (MICCAI 2017). The CNN was tasked with predicting a deformation field that maps the source 2D MV image onto a template 3D CT volume. Using this predicted deformation field, we registered a set of 2D MV images from a radiation therapy case into the corresponding 3D CT planning scan. Results indicate that the proposed method successfully aligns MV and CT images, with registration errors remaining below 2 mm.

The concept of single-particle entanglement, introduced over a decade ago, has recently attracted significant attention, particularly regarding its experimental realization and the investigation of its uniquely quantum characteristics. In this paper, we examine the quantum nonlocality exhibited by single-particle states. We demonstrate that single-particle states display nonlocality by achieving "one-sided device-independent" (1SDI) scenarios, which involve an entangled state composed of a single particle shared between two distant locations. This setup enables local measurements to yield outcomes that are unpredictable even when one agent possesses complete knowledge of their own operations and the other agent uses entirely random, classical strategies. Consequently, single-particle states exhibit a form of "one-sided" (asymmetric) nonlocality, where only one party requires quantum resources while the other can rely on classical means. We further explore the implications of this 1SDI framework, specifically analyzing single-particle steering as a distinct, experimentally accessible manifestation of single-particle nonlocality.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and advanced information technology promises to transform Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) by enhancing the capabilities of autonomous driving and in-vehicle applications within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) frameworks. However, these advancements introduce significant challenges, including security vulnerabilities, privacy concerns, and communication inefficiencies. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized solution that allows multiple participants to collaboratively train models while keeping data local, thereby addressing these issues. Nevertheless, standalone FL faces its own limitations, such as susceptibility to malicious attacks and the high computational costs associated with model aggregation. Blockchain technology provides a robust mechanism to ensure data integrity, secure peer-to-peer communication, and a reliable system architecture. This paper presents a systematic review of blockchain-enabled FL frameworks designed for IoVs, offering a comprehensive taxonomy of existing solutions. Furthermore, it examines open challenges and proposes future research trajectories.

V392 Persei is a well-documented dwarf nova system that unexpectedly underwent a nova eruption in 2012, emitting significant gamma-ray radiation. This study examines multi-epoch observations from Swift-XRT, Chandra, and XMM-Newton, covering the event from shortly after its onset through a year later. The data reveals that the source's X-ray luminosity peaked at approximately $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$ within 1.5 days of the eruption, subsequently declining over roughly 100 days before stabilizing at $10^{35}$ erg s$^{-1}$. The spectral analysis indicates a hard power-law spectrum with a photon index of $\Gamma = 1.8$ during the initial phase, which hardened to $\Gamma = 1.4$ as the luminosity dropped, eventually transitioning to a thermal spectrum after 100 days. The observed X-ray emission aligns with predictions from a standard disk wind model, suggesting the outflow velocity reached $1000$ km s$^{-1}$ within the first 10 days. Additionally, the source exhibited strong variability, with flux fluctuations of a factor of 10 observed within 100 days. The authors propose that the initial hard X-ray emission and rapid variability likely stem from non-thermal processes, potentially involving shocks generated by the interaction between the accretion disk and the nova wind

We examine the impact of introducing two-qubit and higher-order gates on the toric code, contrasting them with findings from prior research on code deformation. Our analysis indicates that these gate operations facilitate the conversion between different dimer configurations within the code's degenerate subspace. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such processes can generate topologically non-trivial loops, which are capable of detecting both non-abelian and abelian anyons.

This work introduces a feedback encoding method utilizing codebook construction via Gaussian mixture model (GMM) for channel state information (CSI) in frequency division duplexing systems. In this approach, channel data is used to train the GMM, which then generates precoding matrix indicators (PMIs) through Bayesian inference. To assess the method, extensive simulations were conducted for both single- and multi-user scenarios across various signal-to-noise ratios. The findings reveal that this GMM-based framework achieves superior channel reconstruction accuracy and outperforms conventional quantization techniques in terms of ergodic mutual information.

Surface currents, defined as robust surface energy flows that endure in systems with zero temperature and finite chemical potential within two-dimensional noninteracting models featuring time-reversal symmetry breaking, have recently garnered significant attention. In this study, we investigate the three-dimensional Hofstadter model and identify a class of surface currents that exhibit even greater robustness. Specifically, these currents persist across a wide range of interaction strengths and are unaffected by disorder, while also remaining stable in the quasi-two-dimensional geometry of a single surface layer. Our analysis indicates that these currents arise from a unique mechanism: a mismatch in the number of surface bands compared to bulk bands, which generates a net current even without orbital magnetization.

The rate of change of Bondi mass $M$ is constrained by the inequality $|\dot{M}|\leqslant\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S}\left|\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}}\right|\mathrm{d}\omega$, where the right-hand side represents the total electromagnetic radiation escaping through null infinity. This result indicates that gravitational wave emission cannot accelerate the reduction of a spacetime's total mass-energy at a rate exceeding that which would occur if this maximum possible electromagnetic radiation were emitted.

We investigate the potential of detecting gravitational waves from Population III remnants within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) using space-based interferometers like LISA. Our findings indicate that the signal strength is significantly contingent on the mass of the most massive black hole (BH) residing in the cluster. Specifically, the spectral amplitude of the gravitational wave background (GWB) generated by a relaxed, N-body system scales as $f_A \propto N^{-1/3}$. Consequently, the signal amplitude for a $10^5 M_{\odot}$ cluster containing a $100 M_{\odot}$ BH is approximately $10^3$ times stronger than that from a system without one, thereby enhancing detectability. Furthermore, the spectral amplitude for a $10^5 M_{\odot}$ cluster with a $1000 M_{\odot}$ BH is roughly $10^4$ times stronger than that of a $10^4 M_{\odot}$ cluster with a $1000 M_{\odot}$ BH. We conclude that GWB detection is feasible for NSCs with masses around $10^5 M_{\odot}$ harboring remnants of first-generation stars, particularly if they contain a BH exceeding $100 M_{\odot}$.

The GECAM satellite mission, developed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, is designed to observe Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and other transient events. This study introduces the design, simulation, and experimental validation of a portable GRB source holder specifically for GECAM. This device enables rapid on-orbit testing of the burst simulator within the satellite's confined environment. Key design considerations included optimizing the holder's dimensions, ensuring electromagnetic compatibility, and guaranteeing compatibility with GECAM's power and data interfaces. Additionally, the paper details the characteristics of the X-ray/GRB simulator and presents the outcomes of its performance evaluation.

We examine semigroups of composition operators acting on the space of analytic functions within the unit disk. Our study centers on characterizing the mean square continuity of $C_{\phi}(t)$, defined by $(C_{\phi}(t)f)(z) = f(\phi_t(z))$, where $\{\phi_t\}_{t\geq 0}$ constitutes a discrete semigroup of self-maps within the unit disk. Additionally, we investigate the continuity of $C_{\phi}(t)$ when mapped from BMOA into $L^2$, as well as its boundedness when acting on various BMOA-type subspaces.

We examine the relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge accumulation, utilizing a model of a knowledge-based economy where an agent's output is driven by their knowledge base, which expands through learning from their own and others' publications. In this framework, the optimal strategy involves a prolonged initial exploration phase, during which the agent freely samples the work of peers to maximize knowledge gain, followed by exploitation of their accumulated insights. We further investigate how an agent's self-interest influences their learning choices within a community context, demonstrating that the model yields knowledgeable, productive, and socially beneficial outcomes.

This paper investigates Physical Layer Security (PLS) within a multi-carrier wireless system involving a source, a destination, and an amplify-and-forward (AF) relay. The study aims to maximize the system's overall secrecy capacity by optimizing the power distribution across all carriers and the signal amplification factor. The optimization framework accounts for both the information leakage directed at an eavesdropper and the available power constraints. Closed-form solutions are derived for the optimal power allocation and the amplifier coefficient. Numerical simulations confirm the validity of these results and demonstrate the superiority of the proposed scheme.

Defining quantum emitters with robust, long-lived states is a central objective in current condensed matter physics research. In this work, we introduce a model featuring two interacting emitters situated within a one-dimensional topological photonic system characterized by a non-trivial $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Chern number. We demonstrate that this setup enables the creation of topological bound states, defined by emitter excitation, which exhibit distinct topological protection. Furthermore, we identify a mechanism to generate multi-mode topological emulators by leveraging the inherent multi-mode nature of these bound states. Finally, we explore the scattering dynamics of photons interacting with these quantum emitters.

Navigating urban intersections remains a significant challenge for connected automated vehicles (CAVs), particularly amidst mixed traffic conditions. Addressing this, we propose a novel predictive control framework tailored for CAVs entering signalized intersections where they coexist with human-driven vehicles (HDVs). This approach integrates a data-driven prediction module with model-based safety-aware predictive control. Specifically, we utilize Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to forecast the future trajectories of HDVs based on real-time traffic data. Leveraging these forecasts, we develop a hierarchical control architecture. The upper layer generates collision-free trajectories for the target CAV by optimizing a comprehensive cost function that accounts for travel time, fuel consumption, emissions, and overall intersection throughput, while ensuring safety through constraints on predicted HDV paths. The lower layer executes these plans via model predictive control (MPC). Extensive simulations demonstrate that this framework significantly enhances both safety and efficiency compared to various baseline methods.

Text-based games serve as an extensive benchmark for language understanding and planning within virtual environments. Although current versions of these environments support a wide range of logic puzzles, their execution speeds are notably sluggish. For instance, running older Minecraft text simulations requires approximately 2,000 steps per second. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance implementation of the original game that achieves a throughput of 100 steps per second. This performance enhancement allows for more thorough stress-testing of artificial agents, which is crucial for effectively evaluating advancements in reasoning capabilities.

Long Short-Term Memory (LMM) networks have emerged as a state-of-the-art solution for video recognition, yet their substantial memory and computational requirements pose significant challenges for efficient deployment on hardware. To address this, we introduce a novel algorithmic and hardware co-design framework that incorporates hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition. This approach enables the simultaneous compression of both memory footprint and computational complexity. Our methodology involves reparameterizing the LSTM's weight tensors and state transitions using Tucker decomposition, which allows for the efficient approximation of the network's hidden states. We further propose a unique hierarchical decomposition strategy that recursively applies Tucker decomposition across LSTM layers and time steps. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves a 3.5× reduction in memory usage and a 2.1× decrease in computational complexity compared to standard LSTM models, with only a negligible impact on recognition accuracy.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks typically require vast amounts of data to achieve high performance, yet in many real-world applications, data availability remains restricted. To mitigate this challenge, researchers have increasingly turned to data augmentation, a technique that expands training datasets by generating new samples from existing ones. However, despite its widespread adoption, a comprehensive review of data augmentation methods in NLP is still lacking. This paper reviews the current landscape of data augmentation strategies for NLP, categorizing them into three main groups: task-agnostic, task-specific, and task-inspired approaches. We provide a thorough examination of each method, analyzing their mechanisms, advantages, and disadvantages. Furthermore, we present an extensive empirical study designed to investigate the efficacy of these augmentation techniques in scenarios characterized by limited data. Our findings indicate that task-agnostic data augmentation methods consistently outperform both task-specific and task-inspired alternatives.

The Weak Gravity Conjecture posits that any theory containing stable Reissner-Nordstr\o{e}m black holes must also include stable particles whose charge-to-mass ratio exceeds that of extremal black holes. This paper investigates the implications of this conjecture within the context of extremal charged black holes. We demonstrate that the entropy of an extremal charged AdS black hole is linearly dependent on its charge squared, $Q^2$. Leveraging the entropy-area law and the AdS/CFT correspondence, we establish that the charge-to-mass ratio squared, $(q/m)^2$, for particles in the dual conformal field theory is bounded from below by a specific constant. We further propose a generalized version of the Weak Gravity Conjecture applicable to any CFT, asserting that $(q/m)^2$ for any such theory must satisfy an inequality of the form $(q/m)^2 \ge (q/m)^2_{\text{ext}}$, where $(q/m)^2_{\text{ext}}$ is determined by the theory's high-temperature behavior.

We propose a model-space framework for simulating the quantum model-space framework, where the Hilbert space is partitioned into subspaces, and the evolution of each model space is governed by an effective Hamiltonian derived within the Schrodinger equation. Building on this effective Hamiltonian formulation, we introduce a model-space quantum imaginary time evolution (MS-QITE) method. This new approach optimizes the coefficients of the corrected Hamiltonian to match the target model-space evolution under imaginary time constraints. We demonstrate that MS-QITE accurately captures complex phenomena, including multi-photon excitations and quantum phase transitions, across diverse systems such as the transverse-field Ising model, Hubbard model, and Frenkel-Ishimori model. By operating directly in model space, MS-QITE achieves a significant reduction in computational overhead compared to traditional QITE methods.

For a local ring $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ with a positive integer $n$ such that $\mathfrak{m}^n = 0$, the tightness of the Hilbert polynomial $P_R(x)$ is defined by the equality $\deg(P_R) = n - 1$. This paper investigates the properties of local rings whose Hilbert polynomials are deemed tight. It is demonstrated that if $R$ is a one-dimensional local ring possessing a parameter ideal $I$ that satisfies the condition $I^2 = \mathfrak{m}I$, then $R$ exhibits the FC (Frobenius closed) property. Furthermore, it is established that a complete intersection local ring $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ of dimension $d > 1$ has a tight Hilbert polynomial if and only if its residue field $R/\mathfrak{m}$ is not isomorphic to $\mathbb{F}_2$ and $d \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ for every parameter ideal $I$. Additionally, the study proves that a two-dimensional local ring $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ is F-rational precisely when its Hilbert polynomial is tight and the socle degree of the associated graded ring $gr_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)$ equals one. Finally, the study provides several new characterizations for F-rationality in F-r

This paper introduces a new ancillary services acquisition model designed to simulate market interactions within the context of policy evaluation. While existing models typically treat these markets as isolated, this approach utilizes a multi-agent framework to represent the broader electricity market. By enabling the simulation of policy scenarios, the model facilitates the assessment of various policy designs. To validate its effectiveness, the authors propose a specific policy aimed at enhancing the integration of renewable energy sources. Their findings indicate that neglecting wider market dynamics when designing ancillary services policies may lead to suboptimal outcomes.

Let $K$ be a field of positive characteristic $p$, and let $f \in K[x]$ be a polynomial such that $f'(x)$ is not a constant in $K[x]$. We demonstrate that there exists a prime number $q$ which divides some prime factor of $p$ for infinitely many integers $n \ge 1$, where $q$ also divides the degree of the $n$-th compositional iterate $f_n(x)$. Furthermore, if $f'(x)$ is not a $p$-th power in $K[x]$, then there is a prime $q$ dividing the degree of $f_n(x)$ for all but finitely many integers $n \ge 1$.

This study employs the matrix element method to isolate signal events from background noise in Higgs boson pair production, specifically within the $h h \to b\bar{b}W W^{*}$ decay channel at the LHC, where one W boson is off-shell. The analysis utilizes the NNLO QCD K-factor and incorporates parton shower Monte Carlo techniques to simulate the $b\bar{b}W W^{*}$ final state. The analysis also simulates the dominant background processes: $t\bar{t}W$, $t\bar{t}b\bar{b}$, $t\bar{t}Z$, $t\bar{t}h$, $Z Z \to b\bar{b}W W^{*}$, and $Z Z \to b\bar{b}Z Z$. The resulting signal-to-background ratio and signal purity are found to be 0.001 and 0.999, respectively.

We investigate extended scalar sectors by analyzing the $e^+e^-\to Zh$ process and Higgs boson decay to photons at the Circular Linear Collider (CLIC). Our study focuses on scenarios where the Standard Model Higgs mixes with additional CP-even scalars, examining how this mixing influences the $H\to\gamma\gamma$ decay rate and the $Z$-boson coupling to fermion-antifermion pairs. We detail the distinct signatures of extended sectors compared to a scenario with a single scalar, utilizing the proposed high-precision measurements from CLIC to probe these extensions.

We demonstrate the existence of local uniform semi-parametric characteristic-$p$ reductions for morphisms between varieties that are defined over a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra which is finitely generated. These results are applied to establish local uniform characteristic-$p$ crystalline deformation functors for specific classes of smooth, proper, and connected varieties under these same conditions.

The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in bulk vanadium dioxide (V$_2$O$_3$) is driven by electron-electron interactions, a phenomenon that can be tuned by modifying the surface termination. Using *ab initio* molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate how surface termination influences the MIT in V$_2$O$_3$(0001) ultrathin films. Our findings reveal that the MIT occurs at a lower temperature for films terminated with oxygen vacancies compared to those with a native termination. Specifically, the MIT temperature ($T_{MIT}$) is approximately 100 K for the vacancy-terminated case, rising to 200 K for the native termination. This temperature difference stems from variations in the on-site Coulomb interaction ($U$) and the electronic bandwidth ($W$) between the two terminations. Furthermore, our results indicate that the MIT temperature is highly sensitive to surface termination, suggesting that engineering the surface termination offers a viable pathway to control the MIT in V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films.

We introduce a novel exact solution for a two-component Bose gas confined in one dimension, featuring two distinct intracompartmental interactions. Our analysis reveals that quantum fluctuations generate stable dark solitons within each compartment, which can interact to form a bound double dark soliton. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical value required for BEC in a dual-component system is significantly influenced by these inter-soliton interactions. Additionally, our findings indicate that the finite-size scaling behavior of the density of the double-component gas exhibits a high degree of accuracy when modeled by its thermodynamic limit.

This paper addresses the determination of normalization constants for measures on manifolds defined by density products. These constants are derived through orbital integrals, which facilitate a comparison between the given measure and one that is uniquely determined by a geometric density.

We introduce a novel spectroscopy technique that merges x-ray scattering with nuclear spectroscopy to overcome the natural limits of spectrometer resolution. This method employs a monochromatized x-ray beam with an initial bandwidth limited only by the source, allowing a high-resolution spectrometer to analyze the scattering spectrum. By applying an inverse algorithm to the recorded data, researchers can reconstruct the high-resolution spectrum of the incident beam. This approach enables the observation of high-resolution features in nuclear scattering, such as natural linewidths, which are typically inaccessible due to spectrometer constraints. Furthermore, the algorithm's flexibility permits the use of various x-ray scattering geometries to extract information about both nuclear and electronic structures.

We introduce a framework for estimating the noise thresholds of quantum error correction (QEC) circuits by employing classical Ising and XY models to simulate the stochastic evolution of logical errors. This approach models the probabilistic noise affecting individual circuit components as an effective classical lattice system, where the resulting thermalization behavior is analyzed to determine the phase of the model. Specifically, the presence or absence of a phase transition indicates whether the encoded logical information is preserved. By constructing realistic representations of the timing and connectivity of QEC circuits, we simulate these classical dynamics to calculate error rates. We validate this methodology by successfully reproducing the known thresholds for the surface code and the Shor code under various noise assumptions. Furthermore, we apply the framework to simulate the "Hades" architecture, demonstrating that its designed connectivity and timing successfully mitigate noise propagation, thereby achieving thresholds significantly higher than those of standard QEC circuits.

Topological insulators represent a novel class of two-dimensional materials characterized by a gapped bulk state and conducting metallic surfaces. This study introduces functionalized tellurene as a prospective 2D topological insulator featuring a substantial band gap. Our investigation employed first-principles calculations to analyze the material's structural, electronic, and magnetic properties. Our findings reveal that pristine tellurene is a zero-gap semiconductor; however, substituting sulfur or selenium atoms at tellurene vacancies induces a significant increase in the band gap, reaching 0.54 eV for sulfur-functionalized and 0.46 eV for selenium-functionalized variants. Furthermore, substituting sulfur or selenium at specific sites can generate magnetic moments of 1 $\mu_B$ per unit cell. Analysis of surface states within the band gap, combined with non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism, confirms the presence of a quantum spin Hall effect in these systems.

This paper introduces a hybridized mixed finite element method designed to model single-phase Darcy flow within fractured porous media. This approach incorporates a newly developed discretization of the governing equations, utilizing a regular mesh for the continuous matrix and a standard unstructured triangular mesh to represent the fracture network. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this method achieves an $O(h^{1.5})$ convergence rate in the $L^2$ norm for velocity and a $O(h^{0.5})$ rate for pressure, assuming a fracture permeability tensor is treated as a regular $L^{\infty}$-bounded coefficient. Numerical experiments validate the method's accuracy and effectively demonstrate its capability to simulate fluid propagation across fractures and into the surrounding matrix.

We present a theoretical investigation into the superconducting spin-valley effect within a structure comprising a superconducting layer adjacent to a ferromagnetic spiral. Our findings demonstrate that this effect occurs regardless of whether the spiral's pitch aligns parallel or antiparallel to the exchange field of the magnetic material. Furthermore, we establish a distinct contrast in the magnetic field dependence of the critical temperature ($T_c$) between these two configurations. Specifically, when the spirals are parallel, the $T_c$ exhibits a "double-dip" pattern as a function of an applied external magnetic field, whereas an antiparallel arrangement yields a simple "single-dip" profile. Additionally, we predict that a magnetic field capable of reorienting the spiral into an antiparallel state can induce a sharp, field-driven transition in the spin-valley effect.

Hypothetical testing serves as a cornerstone of scientific inquiry, with Bayes factors acting as a preferred method for evaluating competing models. Despite this, their widespread application remains limited due to the absence of user-friendly workflow tools and a lack of robustness against prior elicitation choices. This study introduces a novel workflow designed to integrate Bayes factors into broader research contexts. The approach streamlines the comparison of two models by automating the analysis of data, generating posterior distributions, and computing the Bayes factor. Furthermore, it facilitates the systematic examination of sensitivity to various prior specifications. We demonstrate the utility of these methods using a case study on the "missing mass" problem within the Galapagos' finch population.

Discourse markers, such as *however*, *because*, and *for instance*, function to connect ideas and regulate conversation flow. While significant for tasks like machine translation and summarization, current methodologies for their analysis remain inadequate. To address this gap, we introduce **DiscSense**, an automated framework designed to extract semantic information from discourse markers. This framework operates in two stages: initially, it segments these markers from surrounding text using a dedicated detection model; subsequently, it employs a contextualized language model to generate semantic representations for each marker. We evaluated DiscSense on a newly created dataset comprising 1,200 examples of English discourse markers, covering ten distinct semantic categories. The results demonstrate that the framework successfully identifies the semantic roles of these markers with high accuracy.

Defect-based systems in diamond, particularly the negatively charged nitrogen vacancy (NV⁻) center, are highly valued for their ability to sense magnetic and electric fields, as well as temperature. While these defects exhibit distinct optical and spin characteristics, the mechanisms underlying their operation remain only partially understood. This study employs a combination of high-temperature optical spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the structural and optical properties of the NV⁻ center. Our findings reveal that the zero-field zero-phonon line (ZPL) emission at 637.0 nm originates from a structural transition between two configurations: the well-known A-site and a newly identified B-site. The B-site structure is characterized by a shorter N-C bond length of 1.42 Å, compared to 1.47 Å for the A-site, and is stabilized by high lattice temperatures. Consequently, the observed temperature-dependent shift in the ZPL is attributed to a thermally driven population change between these sites rather than a simple thermal expansion effect. Furthermore, the B-site configuration is predicted to exhibit a significantly enhanced spin coherence time, suggesting that the B-site could serve as a more effective platform for future high-temperature quantum sensing applications.

We introduce a local learning rule for supervised training that relies on sparse, overcomplete linear feature extraction. Unlike standard deep learning methods that use dense linear layers to map high-dimensional inputs to low-dimensional representations, our approach matches cortical function by mapping these inputs to an expanded sparse code, which is subsequently compressed via a deep recurrent architecture. The proposed method is implemented as a fully differentiable recurrent neural network trained end-to-end with backpropagation, demonstrating superior performance on the MNIST and EMNIST digit classification tasks compared to standard deep learning baselines. Crucially, we derive a learning rule grounded in perturbation theory that operates entirely within a local architecture, requiring only the immediate neighborhood parameters for updates. This rule achieves digit classification accuracy nearly identical to the original backpropagation-trained model but converges significantly faster. Furthermore, the rule incorporates a mechanism to approximate the non-local gradients produced by backpropagation through local Hebbian interactions, suggesting a viable pathway for implementing biologically realistic supervised learning.

We examine the triangular lattice antiferromagnetic $SU(3)$ spin model, which incorporates a repulsive inter-site interaction among the triplet's color degrees of freedom. This system is mapped onto a nonlinear sigma model, where the constraints imposed by positive-definite interaction strengths result in a model featuring an O(10) symmetry. By applying the large-$N$ approximation to this sigma-model formulation, we determine the ground-state properties of the original $SU(3)$ spin model. Our analysis indicates that strong repulsive interactions drive a transition from a standard Néel ordered state to a novel ordered phase characterized by long-range color order.

A novel approach to solving the Schrödinger and Hartree-Fock equations for arbitrary central potentials is introduced. This method employs B-spline bases to construct the single-particle orbitals and utilizes an iterative algorithm to update the potential self-consistently. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by calculating ground-state properties of atoms, presenting exact potential contours for comparison, analyzing electron gas behavior, and examining the binding energies and structural characteristics of small atomic clusters.

Heterogeneous networks of oscillators can transition from independent behavior to global synchronization through a sudden, explosive change when increasing coupling strength. This paper derives a general criterion predicting such first-order synchronization transitions across various oscillator models. The criterion indicates that if the product of coupling intensity and the ratio of an oscillator's intrinsic frequency sensitivity to its frequency shift yields a value exceeding unity, explosive synchronization will occur. This condition is validated through simulations on both Kuramoto and Rössler oscillator ensembles within scale-free and small-world topologies.

We examine the global optimization landscape of fixed-rank matrix factorization by treating it as geodesic convexity within a specific Riemannian metric space. By establishing an equivalence between the factorization problem and geodesic convexity under this metric, we derive a novel, unified methodology for analyzing the geometry of fixed-rank factorization. Our approach successfully characterizes the geodesic structures of both the Stiefel manifold and the product of Euclidean spaces equipped with a tailored Riemannian metric. Furthermore, we introduce a new class of functions termed "generalized geodesically convex," which encompasses both convex functions and those with generalized convexity properties along geodesics. Leveraging this framework, we demonstrate that fixed-rank matrix factorization is itself generalized geodesically convex. Consequently, these findings indicate that well-established optimization algorithms, such as those relying on local geodesic convexity, are applicable to fixed-rank matrix optimization.

This note presents the initial known counterexample to the conjecture that every cubic bipartite graph requires a chromatic index of at least nine for its edges. Specifically, it demonstrates a graph with chromatic number $\chi'(E') = 7$, thereby contradicting previous expectations.

This paper investigates several new identities involving the functional equation of quadratic Dirichlet $L$-functions. By leveraging the functional equation and specific properties of Gaussian sums, we establish these results.

We examine the stability of particles within Beyond Standard Model (BSM) frameworks, noting that while the Standard Model itself contains an unstable particle, the Higgs boson, a vast array of BSM scenarios also incorporate particles with limited lifespans. We observe that the Standard Model's particle content permits the existence of particles with masses reaching as high as 100 EeV while maintaining stability against vacuum decay. Consequently, we propose that BSM sectors could similarly host particles with comparable masses and short lifespans. We further suggest that the cosmological history might offer a pathway to probe such particles, potentially through the formation of cosmic strings generated by symmetry-breaking phase transitions.

This study examines the low-Reynolds-number motion of a rigid, helical microswimmer embedded in both Newtonian and viscoelastic Carreau fluids. By integrating geometric considerations with the non-linear viscoelastic Oldroyd-B model, we analyze how elastic effects influence the swimmer's trajectory. Our findings reveal that for helical organisms lacking front-back symmetry, viscoelastic environments induce a change in swimming direction, whereas symmetric helical swimmers experience only a reduction in speed without directional deflection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnitude of the normal stress difference within the viscoelastic medium is a critical determinant of the impact on propulsion. Specifically, we show that the maximum velocity reduction occurs when the helix axis aligns parallel to the flow direction, while the most significant directional turning occurs when the axis is oriented at 45° to the flow.

We apply coevolutionary genetic algorithms to determine the Cournot equilibrium in a continuous production game, demonstrating that this approach yields a convergence rate superior to that of standard genetic algorithms. Specifically, within a two-player, two-product framework, we define a "match" as a setup where each player selects an output level for a distinct product, with payoffs determined by the inverse demand function $P(q_1+q_2)=A-B(q_1+q_2)$ and constant marginal costs. In this context, the Nash equilibrium occurs when each player produces half of $(A-c)/B$. We demonstrate that our proposed algorithm converges to this equilibrium state.

The rapid expansion of knowledge sources has heightened the need for automated ontology enrichment, a task that has been addressed using various methods. This study proposes a new approach to automatically extract relationships from unstructured text to enhance ontologies. The method employs a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)-based architecture designed to identify relationships between existing ontology elements. The model is trained on a custom dataset comprising relationship examples derived from the DBpedia and Wikidata knowledge bases. The proposed system is evaluated using a test set of documents from these same knowledge bases, with results indicating that the approach is both effective and efficient.

Although the voter model on a complete graph reaches a dynamic frozen state with extensive order and remains in equilibrium regardless of dimensionality, introducing an Ising-doped variant allows for the investigation of how out-of-equilibrium systems interact with equilibrium ones. By analyzing this modified system, we observe that the dynamics of the underlying voter mechanism drive the Ising subsystem toward equilibrium, a process characterized by a dynamical phase transition. Furthermore, we determine the critical parameters associated with this transition.

The airborne transmission of viruses, such as SARS-CoV-2, is governed by a mix of biological and environmental factors, with weather conditions significantly influencing viral spread. This study employs a computational model to examine how weather affects viral transmission, specifically analyzing the role of relative humidity (RH) on the evaporation rates of respiratory droplets. By analyzing the droplet size distribution resulting from evaporation at various RH levels, the research identifies a peak in the fraction of droplets reaching the inhalable range of 5–10 μm when humidity is approximately 40%. Furthermore, the findings suggest that lower environmental humidity increases the proportion of droplets settling within the optimal inhalable size range, thereby enhancing the potential for viral transmission.

Neural network approaches, including physics-informed variants, are increasingly utilized to resolve partial differential equation (PDE) challenges. Nevertheless, current research lacks systematic evaluation of these methods regarding the representation of uncertainty. This paper reviews and contrasts various uncertainty quantification strategies, categorizing them into aleatoric and non-aleatoric types. We further survey metrics used to assess uncertainty calibration and sharpness. Finally, we evaluate these techniques on two benchmark PDE problems, comparing their performance to traditional methods such as Monte Carlo dropout and the specific adaptations of neural networks for PDEs.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a weighted oriented graph with edge ideal $I(\mathcal{D})$. We demonstrate that for a specified class of oriented trees $\mathcal{D}$, the ordinary and symbolic powers of this ideal are always equivalent. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions ensuring the equality between these powers specifically for lines equipped with their natural orientation within the framework of weighted oriented graphs.

We examine the one-piaulet unitary matrix model under finite dimensions $N$. By applying the iterative method to the discrete $R$-ratio recursion formula, we determine the partition function and its derivatives for all orders where the matrix size is $N=2,3$, and we compare these outcomes against Monte Carlo simulations.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, such as self-driving cars, where hardware faults can cause unpredictable behavior. This study introduces a method to enhance the resilience of object detection models against such hardware anomalies. We propose an activation range supervision (ARS) approach that monitors the output value ranges of neurons within the detection head. During training, ARS learns the expected output range for each neuron by comparing the maximum object scores against the known presence or absence of objects in images. Once established, these ranges are used during inference to detect and correct deviations caused by hardware faults. Experiments on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that ARS significantly improves detection accuracy under memory bit-flip conditions, outperforming other state-of-the-art techniques.

The European Central Bank defines a payment clearing problem as identifying the minimal number of inter-company transfer orders needed to settle all debts, where each order specifies a debtor, a creditor, and a specific amount. This study introduces a novel heuristic algorithm designed to resolve such problems. We evaluated its performance using a novel dataset comprising debt relationships among Romanian entities. Our analysis reveals that the algorithm successfully determined a solution for this dataset, although it did not guarantee an optimal result. Furthermore, we examined how solution quality varies with dataset size and compared our method against a genetic algorithm. Results indicate that the proposed heuristic is significantly faster than the genetic approach while delivering superior solutions.
This paper offers an explicit formula for the $r$-th one-parameter family of Jordanian twists within the constant Jordanian twisted quantum plane.

Cross-lingual common semantic space construction is a fundamental task in natural language processing, yet it remains challenging due to inherent vocabulary discrepancies and distributional variations across languages. To address this, we introduce a new cross-lingual common semantic space using cluster-consistent word embedding. Our approach involves creating a clustering framework that leverages both clustering structures and cluster centers. By enforcing consistency between embeddings and these cluster representations, we establish a unified, shared semantic space. Specifically, we propose a new clustering method called Cluster-Consistent Neural Language Modeling (CC-NLM). CC-NLM builds a clustering model based on neural language modeling, ensuring that the resulting cluster embeddings maintain consistency with the original cluster structures and centers. Finally, we generate cluster-consistent word embeddings by projecting multilingual data into this consistent semantic framework. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches.

We present initial findings from the first high-luminosity, high-energy heavy-ion collisions conducted at the Large Hadron Collider (Cleon), specifically Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV. Using data collected by the ALICE detector, we examine the production yields of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons. These results are analyzed in the context of theoretical models and compared against data from pp interactions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV and Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV.

Dialogue State Tracking (DST) serves as a core component of multi-turn slot-filling systems within intelligent assistants, tasked with monitoring and updating the conversation label across interactions. A significant obstacle in this domain is label noise, which arises from human annotators providing incorrect or inconsistent information. Although recent studies have attempted to address this issue, they often rely on retraining strategies that are constrained by the specific training and validation data splits, limiting their ability to generalize. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a robust framework for noisy-label DST training that utilizes a decoupled curriculum approach. This method employs two distinct models: a domain-specific teacher trained on the validation set to generate clean target labels, and a cleaner student model trained on the noisy data using these generated labels. Experiments conducted on two datasets, including the Noisy Multi-turn DST (NM-DST) benchmark, demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous noisy-label approaches, achieving a 1.5% to 2.5% improvement in Joint Goal Accuracy (JGA).

In response to the Chilean riots of 2019, this study presents a mathematical model grounded in non-local epidemiological frameworks. By incorporating a non-local term that accounts for the travel distance of protesters from their homes to protest sites, the model captures the spatial dynamics of the unrest. We analyze the associated system of non-local partial differential equations and demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the non-local terms can be transformed into a localized system with boundary conditions. Numerical simulations were conducted on both the original non-local formulation and its equivalent localized version to compare their outcomes. The results indicate that the localized system offers superior numerical advantages, making it a more efficient approach for representing the non-local dynamics of the protests.

We examine the reliability of estimating star formation rates (SFRs) for local starburst galaxies by comparing results from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting with those derived from the Brackett-$\gamma$ (Br$\gamma$) luminosity. We analyzed a sample of 100 galaxies from the SPARC database, focusing on nearby systems with precise distance measurements and Br$\gamma$ observations. Our analysis reveals that Br$\gamma$-derived SFRs are systematically lower than those obtained via SED fitting, with a median underestimation factor of 2.5. This discrepancy is likely driven by the inability of Br$\gamma$ to accurately capture the most massive stars, which are often obscured by dust and have lifetimes shorter than the typical resolution of Br$\gamma$ surveys. Consequently, we conclude that SFRs calculated from Br$\gamma$ luminosity are inferior to those derived from SED fitting.

The boundary of the cone of sum of squares (SOS) polynomials contains strictly positive elements, yet characterizing these elements remains an open challenge. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to investigate this topic by introducing the concept of a "minimal" sum of squares representation. We demonstrate that strictly positive polynomials on the boundary of the SOS cone can be constructed from these minimal representations. Furthermore, we propose a conjecture asserting that this class is dense within the broader set of strictly positive polynomials located at the SOS cone's boundary.

We examine the implications of recent findings from the FASER detector, which indicate a non-unitary behavior of the leptonic mixing matrix, potentially arising from physics beyond the Standard Model. By analyzing the constraints on the parameters of the $U(2+2)$ model, we assess the viability of this specific framework. Our analysis reveals that the observed non-unitarity in the lepton sector can be effectively explained by $U(2+2)$, while simultaneously ensuring consistency with existing data from LHC experiments and other relevant measurements.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the containment problem for extended regular expressions, which include expression union, concatenation, Kleene star, and complementation. We demonstrate that by applying Tarski's algorithm for solving boolean algebra equations, the extended expression containment problem can be transformed into a system of these expression components. Applying our methodology yields decidability for the regular expression containment problem under these extended operators.

This paper introduces the VIO-External Memory Attention (VIO-EMA) framework, designed to enhance the robustness of visual-inertial odometry (VIO) using deep learning. The framework consists of two primary modules: a pose estimation network and a velocity estimation network. The VIO-EMA attention mechanism is integrated into the encoder of the pose network to improve feature extraction efficiency. Additionally, the proposed external memory attention mechanism operates on the encoded deep features to generate precise velocity estimates. This approach enables the system to function effectively even when only a single image is available, allowing for the simultaneous provision of reliable pose and velocity data. Extensive experiments conducted on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both pose and velocity estimation.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear operator theory, yet the author suggests that re-examining quantum phenomena through the lens of nonlinear operator theory could yield fresh insights. This work introduces the concept of "higher-order" analogues for well-known properties such as degeneracy, topology, and symmetry breaking by utilizing higher-order differential operators. The results indicate that replacing linear operators with their squared forms allows squared versions of these higher-order phenomena to emerge. Specifically, the investigation identifies four distinct categories of square-root higher-order Weyl nodes, each defined by the intersection of two surface manifolds with differing intersection multiplicities. Furthermore, the study reveals that higher-order topological superconductivity and semimetrical states can be realized via coupling between a higher-order degeneracy and its squared counterpart. Finally, the proposal of a mechanism for symmetry breaking involving a squared higher-order matrix operator is advanced, which may facilitate the generation of additional exotic states of matter.

This paper addresses a data completion problem for time-harmonic Maxwell equations, where a partial electric field measurement is provided on a subdomain of the boundary, and the objective is to determine the complete electromagnetic field throughout the spatial domain. We formulate this as an ill-posed inverse problem and propose a quasi-reversibility method to obtain a stable and convergent solution. Our analysis establishes the existence and uniqueness of solutions derived via this method and demonstrates its convergence toward the solution of the original problem under specific conditions. Furthermore, we derive error estimates contingent upon noise levels in the boundary data. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations.

This manuscript determines the complete set of strong subfactors of the parafermion VOA $K(\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n), k)$, where $n \ge 2$. This finding enables the explicit construction of the corresponding affine symmetrizable Kac–Moody VOAs $W_p(\mathfrak{sl}(n+1))$ via the Zhu algebra $A(W_p(\mathfrak{sl}(n+1))) \cong N(\mathcal{C})$, where $\mathcal{C}$ is the braided tensor category generated by the braided subfactor category $Rep(A(K(\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n), k)))$. Furthermore, we explicitly define the embedding map from $N(\mathcal{C})$ into the Grothendieck ring $K_0(\mathcal{C})$, which is isomorphic to the Kac–Tsuchiya algebra $W_p(\mathfrak{sl}(n+1))$.

Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) is a new framework designed to create a shared representation by merging distributed data from multiple agents. This approach enables agents to collaboratively learn a common model without requiring access to one another's raw data. Unlike traditional federated learning, which trains on individual data silos, FedSA focuses on synthesizing knowledge into a unified model. It operates in two stages: first, a global model is trained using only the parameters sent by agents; second, these parameters are selected based on their alignment with a specific prototype to update the global model. This selection mechanism ensures that only parameters consistent with the prototype are used, thereby preventing negative transfer. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that FedSA converges to a stationary point, and extensive experiments confirm that the resulting model significantly outperforms those trained using only a single agent's data.

Grid cells, discovered over two decades ago, exhibit firing patterns tied to an animal's position within its environment. These cells were initially identified within the hippocampus, yet researchers subsequently located them in the parahippocampal region. This discovery was significant because it revealed that grid cells operate as a spatial mapping system for the brain, functioning as part of the broader hippocampal spatial navigation system. Although grid cells were originally thought to respond exclusively to extrahippocampal inputs, evidence now indicates that specific subfields within the hippocampus also house these cells. We investigate the influence of anti-solar differential rotation on mean-field dynamo models for stars with rotation rates comparable to the Sun's. By analyzing the $\alpha$-effect in Cartesian coordinates, we account for the effects of rotation and magnetic field geometry. Our findings indicate that, within the framework of these dynamo models, such rotational conditions facilitate a magnetic cycle even when the poloidal field generation is too weak to sustain one under solar-like constraints. Specifically, we observe that the $\Omega$-effect can amplify the poloidal field through the interaction between toroidal fields and turbulent magnetic field gradients. This amplification is contingent upon the alignment between the toroidal field and the turbulent gradient, a condition achievable in stars rotating more slowly than the Sun. Consequently, our study suggests that stars exhibiting solar differential rotation patterns are capable of generating magnetic cycles, whereas those with anti-solar patterns are not.

We examine the variation in the ranks of elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ as they extend to the four Galois extensions $S_4$ and $A_4$. By analyzing these curves within the framework of the Birch and Swinerton-Diamond conjecture and employing the Gross-Zagier formula alongside explicit Hecke L-function computations, we establish new findings regarding these rank changes. Our analysis covers both ascending and descending scenarios, yielding several novel theorems. Furthermore, we introduce a new hypothesis concerning the rank growth of elliptic curves under quartic extensions.

The quantum null energy condition (QNEC) establishes a fundamental relationship between the expectation value of the stress-energy tensor and the entropy density on any codimension-two surface. This paper demonstrates that the QNEC serves as a robust lower bound for the rate of entanglement growth following a global quantum quench, applicable to conformal field theories in two and higher dimensions. We derive this bound by analyzing the dynamics of a specific interface in a holographic dual, thereby generalizing earlier results obtained via the gravitational dual. Furthermore, we prove the bound directly within a holographic framework using the covariant Hawking-Kodama-Iyer variational principle. Finally, we propose a new, universal bound governing the initial growth of entanglement in any quantum quench, suggesting it is universal across all quantum field theories.

This study examines the optimal distinguishability time between two quantum states, defined as the minimum evolution duration required for an initial state $\rho$ to become distinguishable from a final state $\sigma$ under a unitary evolution $U(t)$. Specifically, $\tau_{\mathrm{opt}}$ is determined by minimizing the evolution time $t$ such that the trace distance $D(\rho, U(t)\sigma U^{\dagger}(t))$ exceeds a predefined threshold $D$. We demonstrate that this optimal time is governed by the asymmetry of the state pair relative to a specific unitary symmetry group. Leveraging this connection, we establish a quantum speed limit bound based on asymmetry monotones. Furthermore, we analyze quantum evolution restricted to the Bloch ball, deriving a closed-form expression for $\tau_{\mathrm{opt}}$ applicable to arbitrary initial and final states and general Hamiltonians.

Let $X$ be a Banach space, and let $P$ denote a projection onto the subspace of polynomials of degree at most $n$ within $X$, such that for any $f \in X$, the operator norm satisfies $\|P\| \le C n^{\alpha}$. This paper derives an upper bound for the norm of the interpolation projector $Q_n$, defined by $Q_n f \in \Pi_n$ and $Q_n f(x_i) = f(x_i)$ at $n+1$ distinct nodes $x_i \in [0,1]$, assuming the node distribution obeys a specific growth condition.

Superconducting quantum circuits represent a promising avenue for realizing quantum computing and sensing technologies. To advance these fields, it is essential to understand the electromagnetic properties of the constituent materials with high precision. This study employs Terahertz Scanning Near-Field Microscopy (SNFM) to investigate the complex permittivity and permeability of a superconducting quantum processor's substrate and its on-chip resonator. By utilizing a liquid nitrogen-cooled terahertz source, we achieved a spatial resolution of approximately 100 nanometers. Our findings reveal that the permeability of the niobium resonator exhibits a resonant behavior, which is consistent with theoretical models of a two-fluid superconductor.

This paper investigates twisted algebraic $K$-theory within a motivic setting with a twist by an arbitrary invertible object in the $\mathbb{A}^1$-weakly equivalent pointed homotopy category of smooth projective varieties over a field $char \neq 0$. The current atmosphere of Venus is predominantly composed of CO2, with a surface pressure approximately 90 times that of Earth's, and its formation remains a key area of study for understanding planetary atmospheres. This paper examines the evolution of Venus's atmosphere by analyzing the interplay of various processes and mechanisms. It addresses the role of the early atmosphere, the loss of hydrogen and water, the accumulation of CO2, and the lack of a magnetic field in shaping this environment. Furthermore, the work highlights the significance of atmospheric and surface feedback mechanisms, such as the carbonate-silicate cycle, in regulating atmospheric composition. Finally, the authors explore the potential for Venus's atmosphere to have evolved differently than Earth's, and the implications of this research for future missions to the planet.

This study employs reaction nanoscopy to examine the interaction between femtosecond laser pulses and sub-wavelength droplets of 1,2-propanediol (PG), a molecule containing a single hydroxyl group. The research reveals that the size of the emitted electron-ion plasma droplets is governed by the depth of penetration of the electric field within the liquid, whereas the total charge is determined by the number of molecules within the illuminated volume. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the charge-to-size ratio of the droplets can be modulated by adjusting the incident laser intensity.

Whole-slide histopathology images (WSIs) are essential for diagnosing cancer, yet their massive scale and intricate visual details pose significant challenges for automated analysis. To address this, we introduce a novel hierarchical representation that captures both the global context and local features of WSIs. Our method employs a two-stage approach: first, a multi-scale image encoder generates a global representation, while a hierarchical graph encoder constructs a corresponding global structure using tile-level data. Experiments on two major cancer classification datasets demonstrate that this model achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Multivariate point processes are frequently employed to model and analyze events occurring over time, such as financial trades, network traffic, or seismic activity. Within this domain, the Hawkes process stands out as a significant model, particularly in capturing self-exciting behaviors where an event increases the likelihood of subsequent occurrences. A key challenge in this area involves estimating the parameters of nonlinear Hawkes processes, which include both exogenous inputs and endogenous dynamics. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework utilizing variational inference to estimate these parameters from observed event sequences. Specifically, we develop a neural variational inference approach to approximate the joint posterior distribution of latent states and parameters. We validate our methodology through extensive numerical experiments, demonstrating its efficacy in modeling both synthetic data and real-world financial transaction records.

The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is a numerical technique designed to accelerate the calculation of interactions between two discrete sets of points. This approach approximates distant interactions using auxiliary expansions, thereby reducing the computational complexity from quadratic to linear. In this study, we examine the conservation of angular momentum within FMM. We demonstrate that while the method preserves total angular momentum up to an approximation, it fails to conserve its individual components. Consequently, we propose an improved variant of FMM that successfully conserves both the total and all three components of angular momentum.

We introduce a novel semi-supervised domain adaptation framework designed to adapt segmentation models from one anatomical structure to another, utilizing only a limited set of labeled examples for the target structure. Our approach employs contrastive learning to leverage unlabeled data, thereby enhancing the robustness of deep features. Specifically, we utilize a pre-trained segmentation network to generate pseudo-labels for the majority of the source structure instances. These pseudo-labels are then contrastively compared against the actual labels from the few available target structure samples. This strategy ensures that deep features for both structures are pulled closer in the embedding space, while simultaneously pushing features of the target structure apart from those of the unlabeled source data. To further refine these features, we apply self-training using the generated pseudo-labels. Experiments conducted on the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) dataset demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.
